name: HDL cholesterol (HDL-C)
summary: The cholesterol carried in high-density lipoprotein particles. Low HDL-C marks higher cardiovascular risk, but raising it has not been shown to help.
why_it_matters: Low HDL-C is one of the most consistent markers of cardiovascular risk and is part of the metabolic syndrome definition. But it seems to be a marker rather than a cause: genetic studies and drug trials that raised HDL-C did not reduce heart disease, and very high HDL-C is associated with higher, not lower, mortality. It is most useful as a clue to insulin resistance and as an input to risk calculators.

ref_range.source: NCEP ATP III / metabolic syndrome criteria; typical US lab flags
ref_range.note: Many labs use >=40 for both sexes or >=60 as 'high'; >60 mg/dL was historically called a negative risk factor.

deep:
## What it is

HDL particles are small, protein-rich lipoproteins (main protein apoA-I) made by the liver and intestine. They pick up cholesterol from tissues and other lipoproteins and take part in reverse cholesterol transport back to the liver. HDL-C measures the cholesterol mass in these particles, not their number or how well they function, and HDL particles differ widely in size and composition.

## Why it matters

In observational studies, low HDL-C predicts heart disease independently of LDL-C: in the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration (2009), roughly 22% lower coronary risk per 1 standard deviation (about 15 mg/dL) higher HDL-C after adjustment. But the evidence that HDL itself is protective has largely collapsed:

- **Genetics.** A variant in LIPG that raises HDL-C did not lower heart-attack risk, and a genetic score for HDL-C showed no causal link (Mendelian randomization, Voight 2012).
- **Drug trials.** Niacin added to statins did not reduce events (AIM-HIGH 2011, HPS2-THRIVE 2014). CETP inhibitors raised HDL-C dramatically; torcetrapib caused harm, dalcetrapib and evacetrapib showed no benefit, and anacetrapib's modest benefit (REVEAL 2017) was attributed to its lowering of non-HDL cholesterol.
- **Very high HDL-C.** In Copenhagen cohorts, all-cause mortality was U-shaped, with higher mortality at very high HDL-C (in men roughly 97 mg/dL and above; the threshold appeared higher in women, and the exact cut-points are uncertain) (Madsen 2017).

The current reading is that low HDL-C mostly flags the metabolic state (insulin resistance, high triglycerides, excess weight) that travels with it.

## How to read it

Units: mg/dL in the US; divide by 38.67 for mmol/L.

- Below 40 mg/dL in men or 50 mg/dL in women counts toward metabolic syndrome (ATP III, harmonized 2009 definition).
- Women average about 10-15 mg/dL higher than men; US adult means are roughly 48 mg/dL for men and 60 mg/dL for women.
- Being high on the NHANES distribution is not a goal in itself; there is no evidence-based optimal band, and very high values are not reassuring.

## Causes of high

Genetic variants (CETP deficiency, hepatic lipase or LIPG variants); regular alcohol intake; estrogen therapy; vigorous endurance exercise; being lean; primary biliary cholangitis; some drugs (niacin, fibrates modestly, CETP inhibitors).

## Causes of low

Insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome; high triglycerides; obesity; smoking; physical inactivity; very-low-fat high-carbohydrate diets; anabolic steroids and testosterone; progestins; some beta-blockers; acute illness and inflammation; chronic kidney and liver disease; rare genetic disorders (Tangier disease, LCAT deficiency, apoA-I mutations).

## What moves it

Fairly stable within a person (biological variation around 5-10%). Falls during acute infection, surgery or inflammation and recovers afterwards. Rises with alcohol and with exercise training by a few mg/dL; falls with smoking and weight gain. Little affected by fasting. Very high triglycerides can interfere with some direct HDL assays.

## What to test alongside

Triglycerides (the TG/HDL-C ratio is a rough marker of insulin resistance), LDL-C, non-HDL-C and apoB, fasting glucose, insulin and HbA1c, waist circumference and liver enzymes.
